message.content:
**Decision: do not deploy this as a tenant-isolation boundary.** The documentation forbids that use, and several specific assumptions are wrong.

**Incorrect premises**

1. *"Sole tenant-isolation boundary."* The model "does not protect against malicious code… Malicious code can bypass the permission model and execute arbitrary code without the restrictions imposed" ([permissions.html#permissions](https://nodejs.org/download/release/v24.21.0/docs/api/permissions.html#permissions)). SECURITY.md states `--permission` "is designed to reduce the blast radius of mistakes in trusted application code, **not** to act as a security boundary against intentional misuse or a compromised process" ([SECURITY.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nodejs/node/v24.21.0/SECURITY.md), "Permission Model Boundaries (`--permission`)").
2. *Staging on `--permission-audit` proves nothing about production:* audit mode performs no denial — violations are only published to diagnostics channels — and if both flags are passed, `--permission` wins ([#audit-mode](https://nodejs.org/download/release/v24.21.0/docs/api/permissions.html#audit-mode)).
3. *`--allow-fs-read=/srv/jobs/*.js` does not restrict to `.js`:* "After passing a wildcard character (*) all subsequent characters will be ignored," so it behaves as `/srv/jobs/*` ([#file-system-permissions](https://nodejs.org/download/release/v24.21.0/docs/api/permissions.html#file-system-permissions)).
4. *Relative symlinks in job directories are a documented hole:* "Symbolic links will be followed even to locations outside of the set of paths that access has been granted to. Relative symbolic links may allow access to arbitrary files" ([#limitations-and-known-issues](https://nodejs.org/download/release/v24.21.0/docs/api/permissions.html#limitations-and-known-issues)). Untrusted-writable job dirs therefore defeat the read list.
5. *`--env-file` is outside the model* (loaded before permission initialization), so secrets land in `process.env` readable by the job ([#permission-model-constraints](https://nodejs.org/download/release/v24.21.0/docs/api/permissions.html#permission-model-constraints)); and *passing an open fd bypasses the model entirely* ("Using existing file descriptors via the node:fs module bypasses the Permission Model").
6. `--allow-worker` also exposes ungated `process._debugProcess(pid)` ([#process_debugprocess](https://nodejs.org/download/release/v24.21.0/docs/api/permissions.html#process_debugprocess-and-cross-process-inspector-activation)).

**Worker inheritance — genuinely conflicting, UNVERIFIED.** permissions.html says "The model does not inherit to a worker thread" ([#permission-model-constraints](https://nodejs.org/download/release/v24.21.0/docs/api/permissions.html#permission-model-constraints)), while SECURITY.md says "Workers inherit the permission restrictions of their parent process… Passing an empty or modified `execArgv` does not grant additional permissions." worker_threads.html only says `execArgv` is inherited by default ([worker_threads.html#new-workerfilename-options](https://nodejs.org/download/release/v24.21.0/docs/api/worker_threads.html#new-workerfilename-options)). Do not assume exact inheritance; resolve via the v24.21.0 test suite or a Node.js issue.

**Recommendation (not documented fact):** use separate OS users/containers, seccomp/AppArmor, and per-tenant process isolation, as the same page suggests; keep the Permission Model as defense-in-depth for trusted code only. **No, these documents do not let you certify tenant isolation.**
message.reasoning_content:
Now I have two pages. Key conflicting evidence:

1. permissions.html "Permission Model constraints" says: "The model does not inherit to a worker thread." But SECURITY.md says "worker_threads with modified execArgv: Workers inherit the permission restrictions of their parent process. Passing an empty or modified execArgv to a worker does not grant it additional permissions." And worker_threads.html says "Worker threads inherit non-process-specific options by default... execArgv by default inherited from parent thread."

So conflicting. That's the UNVERIFIED limitation. Good.

2. --permission-audit vs --permission: audit mode does not deny. Staging with audit mode gives zero enforcement — no isolation at all, so staging tests would be meaningless as isolation evidence. Also if both specified, --permission takes precedence.

3. --allow-fs-read=/srv/jobs/*.js — wildcard truncation: "After passing a wildcard character (*) all subsequent characters will be ignored. For example: /home/*.js will work similar to /home/*." So the literal argument */srv/jobs/*.js is equivalent to /srv/jobs/* — granting read to everything in the directory including non-.js files.

4. Symlinks: "Symbolic links will be followed even to locations outside of the set of paths that access has been granted to. Relative symbolic links may allow access to arbitrary files and directories." Also SECURITY.md says symlink resolution within allowed list is intended behavior, not a bypass. So relative symlinks in job dirs = a bypass of read restriction → premise "job directories may contain relative symbolic links" is a real hole, not a minor issue.

5. --env-file: "certain flags such as --env-file or --openssl-config are designed to read files before environment initialization. As a result, such flags are not subject to the rules of the Permission Model." So reading env file outside read list works but also means env-file contents are outside the model — and env is readable by the job (process.env), so secrets in env-file are accessible to untrusted code. Also note job code gets process.env.

6. Already-open file descriptor: "Using existing file descriptors via the node:fs module bypasses the Permission Model." So passing an already-open fd means the job can read/write through that fd regardless of permissions — if it's a write fd or a directory fd, that's a hole. Actually in fs.readFile(fd) etc.

7. Sole tenant-isolation boundary: docs explicitly say "This feature does not protect against malicious code... Node.js trusts any code it is asked to run... does not provide security guarantees in the presence of malicious code. Malicious code can bypass the permission model and execute arbitrary code without the restrictions." SECURITY.md: "designed to reduce the blast radius of mistakes in trusted application code, not to act as a security boundary against intentional misuse or a compromised process." So the answer: No, cannot certify tenant isolation. Wrong premise.

8. process._debugProcess() not gated — untrusted job can force another Node process to open inspector, under same OS user. Recommend different OS users.

9. --allow-worker: needed to use worker_threads. Fine, but the worker inheritance question is contradictory.

Also: OS-level isolation recommended (separate OS users, seccomp/AppArmor). Also note Node license: the permission model restricts inspector, native addons, WASI.

Also `--permission` restrict all: native addons, child process, worker threads, inspector, fs, WASI.

Let me also consider the audit-mode caveat for staging: staging with --permission-audit means access isn't denied, so effective isolation in staging is zero. Also audit mode useful for discovering needed permission.
